references.citation_apa: Andrews-Hanna**: The neural substrate for Extent is primarily the medial temporal DMN subsystem — specifically, the hippocampal *scene construction* function (Hassabis & Maguire, 2007). When the hippocampus constructs a rich, coherent scene model (high scope + high coherence), the result is a sense of immersion — "being in a whole other world." This scene construction process engages the hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and retrosplenial cortex, all of which are medial temporal DMN nodes

Brainard**: L2 is the closest to calibrated. We have the action spectrum (peak ~480nm), we have dose-response curves for melatonin suppression (Brainard et al., 2001), we have the CS metric with specific thresholds (CS ≥ 0.3 for ≥ 2 hours; Rea et al., 2021), and we have the CIE S 026 standard for melanopic irradiance measurement. When Article Eater encounters a finding about circadian disruption in a building, L2 can ask: "What was the melanopic irradiance? At what time? For how long?" and compare against calibrated dose-response predictions. That is a template that can actually catch a bad study — one that claims circadian benefits from a light intervention that delivers sub-threshold melanopic stimulus

Critical experiment**: Select pairs of buildings matched for total path length but differing in PE event density (e.g., a winding museum with many room transitions vs. a long gallery with few). Fit visitors with eye-tracking and movement sensors to measure PE events (fixation changes, gait adjustments, spatial transitions). After the visit, collect prospective time estimates, retrospective time estimates, and number-of-events estimates. Predict: PE event density correlates with retrospective duration estimation (Wittmann, 2016) and with number-of-events recalled

Gehl**: SC4's claim that spatial configuration determines social encounter conditions is supported by fifty years of observational research. The relationship between spatial integration and pedestrian density is empirical. The PE interpretation — that social encounters are social PE events whose valence depends on spatial context — is new but entirely consistent with the social brain literature. The open-plan office case (high visual connectivity → chronic social monitoring → attention fatigue) is well-documented by Kim and de Dear (2013) among many others

Gigerenzer**: MAT5 (material-cultural conditioning) is well-supported by the general evaluative conditioning literature (Reber et al., 2004; De Houwer, Thomas, & Baeyens, 2001) but has almost no architectural-specific evidence. We know that learned associations affect material preferences — marble "means" luxury, raw concrete "means" brutalism — but the specific learned associations, their cross-cultural variability, and their interaction with the sensory mechanisms have not been systematically studied. This is our most preliminary template
